new_statements.quote: [Burung 2000:9] Nevertheless, it was observed in the word list that on bisyllabic words, stress is not predictable on the basis of position in the word. ... It may not be the case that stress is penultimate, since on trisyllabic words it is also not predictable. ... Further it was noticed that schwa may carry stress. ... From the above list, it may be suggested that stress in Elseng is unpredictable and upon further studies it is to be marked in any wordlist [Voorhoeve 1971:72, Morwap] Bi-syllabic words generally have stress on the last syllable, tri-syllabic words have secondary stress on the first and primary stress on the third syllable.
new_statements.citation: Burung, Wiem. 2000. A Brief Note on Elseng. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2000-001. Dallas: SIL International (p.9, sec. 1.3; endnote 8 p.16); contrasting statement: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1971. Miscellaneous notes on languages in West Irian, New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics A-28: 47-114 (p.72, sec. 2.4 'The Morwap language').
new_statements.locator: Burung 2000: p.9 (page footer), section 1.3 'Suprasegmental properties: Metrical stress and Intonation', with endnote 8 on p.16. Voorhoeve 1971: p.72, section 2.4, paragraph after the consonant chart.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The two primary sources conflict. Voorhoeve 1971 (survey wordlists, 'tentative analysis'): word stress is final -- disyllables generally stressed on the last syllable, trisyllables primary stress on the third syllable with secondary stress on the first. Burung 2000 (6 h with one displaced speaker): stress position is not predictable in di- or trisyllables (examples with initial, medial and final stress), schwa can bear stress, so stress should be marked lexically; his own stress-marked 209-item list is dominated by initial (= penultimate) stress in disyllables (c. 59 vs 9 final), which he suspects reflects Indonesian influence on the speaker (endnote 8).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Voorhoeve 1971: trisyllables carry secondary stress on the first syllable (primary on the third). Burung 2000: nothing on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Voorhoeve: 'generally' (no exceptions listed). Burung: cites 'mEkEn 'liver' vs ti'tan 'straight' (disyllables), 'wçmbiak 'head', 'ukmçlçf 'fat', a'lautan 'dirty', k´k´'laf 'hand' (trisyllables), and stressed schwa in 's´pak 'foot', 'm´k´n 'know', 'm´nai 'what'; endnote 8: 'My personal impression is the informant's pronunciation is influenced by the Indonesian stress pattern - which is always penultimate except when the schwa falls on the penultimate syllable - while trying to produce his native words.'
new_statements.domain_note: Both statements concern isolated elicited words (survey wordlist citation forms). Burung separately notes phrase-level rising/falling intonation (interrogative vs statement) from two items; no claim about phrasal stress. Burung's speaker had left the Elseng area 20 years before recording and used Indonesian and Kemtuk daily.
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve 1971 and Laycock 1973 call the language Morwap (formerly Sawa, or Tabu); Burung 2000 calls it Elseng [»ElsEN] (alternate names Tabu/Tapu) and quotes Ethnologue's MORWAP (JANGGU, DJANGGU, ELSENG, TABU, SAWA) entry as the same language. All refer to Glottolog else1239 / ISO mrf; no dialect glottocodes exist. Burung's data come from one speaker from Omon village (Kemtuk-Gresik/Kaure districts) who left the area in 1978 and was recorded in Sentani in 1998; Voorhoeve's Morwap data are survey wordlists from the Sawa-area villages (Jamas, Kasso, Penemon, Samsai, Sawa).
